title: Remote Repositories
description: Working with GitHub, GitLab, and Bitbucket

content.overview: Remote repositories allow you to collaborate with others and back up your code. In this module, you'll learn how to work with remote repositories on platforms like GitHub, GitLab, and Bitbucket.

steps.title: Understanding Remote Repositories
steps.content: A remote repository is a version of your project that is hosted on the internet or network somewhere. Collaborating with others involves managing these remote repositories and pushing and pulling data to and from them.

steps.title: Viewing Remote Repositories
steps.content: You can view the remote repositories associated with your local repository using the `git remote` command.

behindTheCommand.title: How Git Tracks Remotes
behindTheCommand.content: Git stores information about remote repositories in the `.git/config` file. Each remote has a name (commonly 'origin') and a URL. When you run `git remote`, Git reads this configuration file to display the remote names. The `-v` flag shows the URLs associated with each remote.

steps.title: Adding a Remote Repository
steps.content: You can add a remote repository using the `git remote add` command followed by the remote name and URL.

behindTheCommand.title: What Happens When Adding a Remote
behindTheCommand.content:
When you add a remote, Git updates the `.git/config` file with the new remote information. This includes the remote name, URL, and fetch specifications. No connection is made to the remote repository at this point; Git simply records the information for future use.

The remote name is a shorthand that you'll use in other Git commands to refer to the remote repository. By convention, the primary remote is usually named 'origin', but you can use any name you prefer.

steps.title: Fetching from a Remote
steps.content: The `git fetch` command downloads objects and refs from a remote repository without merging them into your local branches.

behindTheCommand.title: What Happens During Fetch
behindTheCommand.content:
When you run `git fetch`, Git contacts the remote repository and retrieves all the objects and refs that you don't have yet. This includes new branches, commits, and tags. The objects are stored in your local repository's object database, and the refs are stored in `.git/refs/remotes/[remote-name]/`.

Importantly, `git fetch` doesn't modify your working directory or local branches. It simply downloads the data and updates your remote-tracking branches (e.g., `origin/main`). This makes it a safe operation that won't interfere with your local work.

steps.title: Pulling from a Remote
steps.content: The `git pull` command fetches from a remote repository and integrates the changes into your current branch.

commands.description: Pull from the 'main' branch of the 'origin' remote

behindTheCommand.title: What Happens During Pull
behindTheCommand.content:
The `git pull` command is essentially a combination of two operations:

1. `git fetch` - Downloads objects and refs from the remote repository
2. `git merge` or `git rebase` - Integrates the changes into your current branch

By default, `git pull` uses merge to integrate the changes. This creates a merge commit if there are divergent changes. You can configure Git to use rebase instead with `git pull --rebase` or by setting the `pull.rebase` configuration option.

Unlike `fetch`, `pull` does modify your working directory and current branch to incorporate the remote changes.

steps.title: Pushing to a Remote
steps.content: The `git push` command uploads your local branch commits to a remote repository.

commands.description: Push the 'main' branch to the 'origin' remote

behindTheCommand.title: What Happens During Push
behindTheCommand.content:
When you run `git push`, Git contacts the remote repository and sends the objects and refs that the remote doesn't have yet. This includes commits, trees, and blobs. The remote repository then updates its refs (branches or tags) to point to the new commits.

For a push to succeed, your local branch must be ahead of the remote branch, meaning it contains commits that the remote doesn't have. If the remote has commits that you don't have (i.e., someone else has pushed changes), Git will reject your push. In that case, you need to pull the remote changes first, integrate them with your work, and then push again.

steps.title: Working with GitHub
steps.content: GitHub is one of the most popular platforms for hosting Git repositories. Let's look at some GitHub-specific workflows.

behindTheCommand.title: GitHub Workflow
behindTheCommand.content:
GitHub provides a web-based interface for Git repositories, along with additional features like pull requests, issues, and actions. A typical GitHub workflow involves:

1. **Forking a repository** - Creating your own copy of someone else's repository
2. **Cloning your fork** - Downloading your fork to your local machine
3. **Creating a branch** - Making a new branch for your changes
4. **Making changes** - Editing files and committing your changes
5. **Pushing to your fork** - Uploading your changes to your GitHub fork
6. **Creating a pull request** - Requesting that the original repository incorporate your changes

This workflow allows for collaboration while maintaining control over who can directly modify the main repository.

steps.title: Cloning a Repository
steps.content: The `git clone` command creates a copy of a remote repository on your local machine.

commands.expectedOutput:

remote: Counting objects: 100% (100/100), done.
remote: Compressing objects: 100% (80/80), done.
remote: Total 100 (delta 20), reused 90 (delta 10), pack-reused 0
Receiving objects: 100% (100/100), 10.00 KiB | 5.00 MiB/s, done.

behindTheCommand.title: What Happens During Clone
behindTheCommand.content:
When you run `git clone`, Git performs several operations:

1. Creates a new directory for the repository
2. Initializes a new Git repository in that directory
3. Adds a remote named 'origin' pointing to the URL you provided
4. Fetches all objects and refs from the remote repository
5. Creates local branches that track remote branches (usually just 'main' or 'master')
6. Checks out the default branch (usually 'main' or 'master')

After cloning, you have a complete copy of the repository, including all its history. The local branches are set up to track their remote counterparts, making it easy to push and pull changes.

steps.title: Working with Multiple Remotes
steps.content: You can work with multiple remote repositories by adding them with different names.

behindTheCommand.title: Managing Multiple Remotes
behindTheCommand.content:
Working with multiple remotes is common in open-source development, where you might have your own fork of a repository as well as a reference to the original repository. By convention, the original repository is often called 'upstream'.

With multiple remotes, you can:

1. Push your changes to your own fork (`git push origin feature-branch`)
2. Keep your fork updated with changes from the original repository (`git pull upstream main`)
3. Create pull requests from your fork to the original repository

This setup gives you the flexibility to contribute to projects while maintaining your own copy of the code.
